prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which established the biological basis for incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024 as a single part, credited to Holst, Mojsov and Drucker. I took the chair's question about easy defaults seriously and tested B024 against the two strongest rivals on the criteria that matter to me: originality of the discovery, clarity of the mechanism, independence of confirmation, and how cleanly credit can be assigned. B011 has comparable clinical force but a structurally larger attribution gap (Eshhar and the early chimeric receptor work are outside the credited names) and the Rosenberg question. B020 is a clean mature pair with a very clear mechanism, but its translational payoff is thin and the Ron branch is outside the credited names. B024 is the only candidate where the full chain from proglucagon processing, through the truncated active peptide and its glucose-dependent and satiety actions, to randomized outcome trials in glycemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints is continuous and replicated independently over decades. The three credited names map to separable discovery steps: Holst on the physiology of the active peptide, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active form, Drucker on the peptide biology and the therapeutic concept. That is the comparison that shows the near-unanimity reflects relative merit; I am not relying on the count.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the real weakness and I do not think round 1 resolved it. The priority picture for the active GLP-1 peptide involves the Habener group, who are not on the supplied credited list, and Mojsov is the least secure of the three slots. I cannot settle the primary-paper dates from the supplied record, so I treat this as an open risk and not as something I have checked. Excluding Knudsen is a real cost: the acylation-based half-life extension is original inventive science and is what put the drug in patients, so a prize limited to the physiology can be read as honouring the discovery but not the medicine. The three-person ceiling forces that choice, and I accept that it is a judgement about what kind of achievement we are rewarding and not a neutral scientific verdict.

responses.point: Keep Mojsov but have the committee examine the primary papers and dates before the final ballot; if the review fails, move toward a Holst and Drucker pair and do not substitute a weaker third name.
responses.response: I agree that the review is necessary, and I would add what would count as sufficient: contemporaneous publication of the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide form, and independent evidence that its insulinotropic activity was established, not only claimed. Where I differ slightly is the fallback. A two-person Holst and Drucker prize with no third name is defensible, but the vacant slot is exactly where Knudsen would then fit, so I would not rule out a Holst, Drucker and Knudsen configuration if Mojsov's priority fails. That would change the character of the prize toward discovery plus development, and the citation would have to say so. On the evidence available to me now I do not think the review fails, so I hold the trio, but I would not call the third slot closed.

responses.point: Knudsen's exclusion is not only a space problem: the Nobel logic is a discovery that changed medicine, the hormone physiology is the discovery, and half-life engineering is development built on it.
responses.response: I partly move toward you. In round 1 I framed her exclusion mainly as a consequence of the three-person ceiling. I now think the principled reason is better stated as you put it: the incretin physiology and the identity of the active peptide are what created the possibility of the drug class, and each of the three names is decisive for a different step. I still disagree that development is categorically lesser, because the committee has honoured translational invention before, so the citation should not imply the drugs were trivial. We agree on the practical conclusion that the citation must name physiology and the active peptide concept and not products. Your point that a visible gap remains in the narrative is correct, and I would rather state it openly than hide it.

responses.point: If the review of the Mojsov and Habener record fails, the vacated place would naturally go to Knudsen, which changes the character of the prize; the basic-science trio is otherwise the most defensible fit.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional and with your reason for leaving Knudsen out of the base configuration. I would go one step further and say we should decide now what we do under each outcome, so that the final ballot does not turn on an unspoken judgement about the kind of achievement. My position: if Mojsov's slot is sustained, the trio stands and Knudsen is outside it. If it is not, I would prefer Knudsen over leaving the place empty or adding a weaker name, accepting that the prize then recognises physiology and development together. On B045, I listed it as an alternative in round 1, but your own caution about proximity to your field and the six claimants against three slots persuade me it is not a robust fallback, so I have moved my second alternative.

responses.point: A second part such as B020 would force the three-person limit to produce a worse GLP-1 trio, so Walter and Mori are better treated as an alternative; Ron's PERK and integrated stress response work also sits outside the credited list.
responses.response: I agree and this is why B020 is an alternative and not a second part in my configuration. A two-part prize would require at most three people overall, which would break the incretin trio or leave B020 with a single name, and that is a worse outcome on both sides. I have replaced B045 with B020 as my second alternative because the Walter and Mori pairing is cleaner to attribute than six optogenetics claimants, even though I accept your point about its thin translational payoff. I also note that your reading of my opening ranking is partly out of date: in my opening I did favour Rosenberg as a third CAR-T name, but I no longer do, for the reasons you give about citation clarity.

responses.point: Anchor B024 on the discovery that opened the incretin field, and treat drug development as a separate achievement if the committee wants to honour it; Rosenberg's work is a conceptual foundation but the engineered receptor and clinical translation are the decisive step for B011.
responses.response: On B011 we now agree: the June and Sadelain pair is the clean form, and I withdraw my earlier support for a third Rosenberg slot. The cost is that the Eshhar omission becomes more visible, and I would not claim that two names resolve it, which is why B011 stays an alternative and not my preferred part. On B024 I accept your anchoring on discovery, but I do not agree that a separate Knudsen achievement is practical this year: the shortlist offers no separate development part, and a second part would break the three-person ceiling. So the real choice is between the trio and a fallback that substitutes Knudsen, and I would make that choice on the primary-paper review you and the chair's questions point to.

uncertainties: Whether the contemporaneous record supports limiting credit for the active GLP-1(7-36) form to Mojsov, given the parallel work of the Habener group, which I have not been able to verify from the supplied material.
Whether the committee will treat drug development as part of the achievement; if so, Knudsen would replace one of the three names and the citation would change.
Whether the Eshhar and early chimeric receptor omission is a sufficient reason to keep B011 behind B024, as I currently judge it.
Long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy are still being characterised, though I do not regard this as a maturity concern.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on B024, B011 or B020. As previously disclosed, I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen at Karolinska Institutet and did RNA-processing work with the Burge group at MIT; none of these people is a credited name on a shortlisted candidate. This note is unchanged from round 1.
